Follow these writing rules. They matter as much as the content:

- Bold used as body emphasis throughout -- reserve bold for a rare callout
- A short rhetorical question with a canned answer -- collapse into one direct statement
- Short buildup, then a reveal: "The best part: it learns." -- state it as a plain sentence
- Emoji or decorative checkmarks in body text -- cut them
- An em dash, section sign or middle dot written as an HTML entity -- write the plain character
- Throat-clearing openers: "needless to say", "at the end of the day" -- state the point directly from the first sentence
- Fake ID tags opening list items: "R-1.", "US-01" -- number the list plainly
- Marketing adjectives: seamless, robust, cutting-edge -- say what is actually true
- The "not just X but Y" construction -- make the point once
- Body paragraphs nearly identical in length -- vary them with what each paragraph has to do
- A significance clause bolted to a sentence: ", underscoring the..." -- delete it, or make it a claim with something behind it
- Three parallel -ing items in a series -- keep the one that carries information
- Fake-humility feedback requests: "would love your feedback on this" -- cut them
- Horizontal rules dropped between sections -- headings already separate sections
- Headings Capitalised Like This -- sentence case
- Vague intensifiers with no number behind them: very, really, quite, significantly -- say how much, or cut the word
- Unnamed authority: "studies show", "experts agree" -- name the actual source, or cut the claim

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write a comparison of two approaches to background jobs: a queue with workers, and scheduled batch runs. Around 200 words.

A queue with workers and a scheduled batch run solve the same problem at different latencies, and the choice usually comes down to how long a piece of work can sit untouched.

The queue is the right shape when arrival is unpredictable and someone is waiting on the result. A user uploads an image, a job lands on the queue, a worker picks it up within a second. Workers scale by adding processes. The cost is operational surface: a broker to run, retry and dead-letter policy to define, poison messages to handle, and enough idle worker capacity to absorb bursts. Debugging is harder too, since a failure is spread across a producer, a broker, and a consumer that may have died mid-message.

Batch runs trade latency for simplicity. A cron entry fires a script at 03:00, the script queries for pending rows, processes them in one pass, and exits. There is no always-on infrastructure and one place to look when it breaks. Batching also makes some work cheaper: one bulk API call instead of ten thousand individual ones. The failure mode is that a run can overrun into the next window, and a bad night means work sits for 24 hours.

Plenty of systems run both: a queue for anything user-facing, a nightly batch for reconciliation and cleanup.

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Add a paragraph on what happens when a job fails in each.

Failure is where the two diverge most. In a queue, a failed job is a message that gets returned to the broker and retried on a backoff, usually three or five times before it lands in a dead-letter queue. That isolates the damage: one bad message does not stop the other ten thousand. It also means you need somewhere to look at dead-lettered messages and a person who looks there, or failures accumulate silently for weeks. Retries also demand idempotent handlers, since a worker that dies after doing the work but before acknowledging the message will have that work redone.

A batch run tends to fail all at once. An unhandled exception halfway through the loop leaves the first half processed and the second half untouched, and unless the script tracks per-row state, the next night's run either reprocesses the first half or skips the second. The fix is to write the batch as if it will crash: mark each row as it completes, wrap the loop body so one bad row is logged and skipped rather than fatal, and make the whole run safe to re-execute. Batch failures are also quieter. A cron job that exits non-zero at 03:00 tells nobody unless you wired up an alert, and the first sign of trouble is a customer asking where their report went.

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Add a recommendation for a small team.

For a team of three to five engineers, start with the batch run and add a queue only when something forces you to. A cron entry plus a script that marks each row done covers reconciliation, report generation, cleanup, and most email sends, and it costs you no broker to patch, no worker fleet to keep alive at 3 a.m., and no separate retry semantics to reason about. Write it re-runnable from the first commit and you have handled most of what a queue would have given you.

Reach for the queue at the point a user is watching a spinner. If someone submits a form and needs the result inside a few seconds, cron cannot help, and no amount of tightening the schedule turns a batch into a queue. That is the line: batch for work with a deadline measured in hours, queue for work with a deadline measured in seconds.

When you do add one, use whatever your existing infrastructure already provides. If you run Postgres, a table with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` gets you a working queue with no new service. If you run Redis, use it. A small team that adds a dedicated broker gains one more thing to monitor and upgrade, and the failure will arrive on a weekend. Buy the latency only when you need it, and buy it with the cheapest infrastructure that delivers it.

For a team of three to five engineers, use the batch run. A cron entry plus a script that marks each row done covers reconciliation, report generation, cleanup, and email sends. It costs you no broker to patch, no worker fleet alive at 3 a.m., no second set of retry semantics to hold in your head. Write it re-runnable from the first commit and you have what a queue would have given you.

Add a queue the day a user is watching a spinner. If someone submits a form and needs the result in three seconds, cron cannot deliver that, and tightening the schedule to every minute does not change the answer. That is the line: batch for work with a deadline in hours, queue for work with a deadline in seconds. Nothing else on the list of reasons to adopt a broker holds up.

When you cross that line, use the infrastructure you already run. On Postgres, a jobs table with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` is a working queue and costs you one migration. On Redis, use Redis. Do not stand up RabbitMQ or SQS for your first queue; you will spend the next year monitoring and upgrading it, and the outage will land on a Saturday. Buy latency when a user is paying for it, and buy it from the database you already back up.
